questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Oxygen Transport and Hemoglobin
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with chronic gastrointestinal bleeding whose hemoglobin is 6.4 g/dL. The client reports fatigue and becomes short of breath walking to the bathroom. HR 118/min, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air. The client asks, “Why can’t I breathe when my oxygen number is perfect?” Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “The oximeter is reading falsely high because your fingers are so pale and cool.”
“Your lungs are not moving enough air in and out to meet your needs.”
“There is too little hemoglobin to carry enough oxygen, even though it is saturated.”
“Your breathing is fast because carbon dioxide is building up in your bloodstream.”
optionRationales: Pallor does not make the oximeter read falsely high. SpO₂ correctly reports the percentage of available hemoglobin that is saturated; the problem is the total amount of hemoglobin.
Nothing suggests a ventilation problem. The client is moving air well enough to keep the available hemoglobin fully saturated.

Correct. SpO₂ is a percentage. When hemoglobin is 6.4 g/dL, 98% of a small supply is still too little oxygen for the tissues. The body compensates with tachycardia and tachypnea, and the client develops dyspnea on exertion.
Anemia does not cause CO₂ retention. The tachypnea is compensation for low oxygen delivery to tissues, not hypercapnia.
questions.rationale: Oxygen delivery depends on hemoglobin concentration, saturation, and cardiac output. Pulse oximetry measures only the percentage of hemoglobin that is saturated (SaO₂/SpO₂), not how much oxygen the blood actually carries. In severe anemia, SpO₂ can be normal while tissues are hypoxic. That is why the client has tachycardia, tachypnea, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea.
questions.takeaway: A normal SpO₂ does not rule out tissue hypoxia when there is too little hemoglobin.
questions.hintContent: Recall what SpO₂ actually measures: a percentage of hemoglobin, not the total amount of oxygen in the blood.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the option that explains the mismatch between a normal number and abnormal symptoms. Rule out options that add a problem the data do not support.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Ventilation–Perfusion Relationships
questions.stem: A client who is 3 days postoperative after a total knee arthroplasty suddenly reports shortness of breath and says, “Something is wrong.” RR 30/min, HR 124/min, SpO₂ 88% on room air. Breath sounds are clear bilaterally, chest expansion is symmetrical, and there is no cough. Which explanation for the client’s hypoxemia is most likely?
options: Alveoli are ventilated, but blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries is blocked
Alveoli have collapsed from shallow breathing, so blood passes unventilated alveoli
Air has entered the pleural space and collapsed part of the lung
Fluid has filled the alveoli and is blocking diffusion of oxygen
optionRationales: Correct. Sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, anxiety, and hypoxemia with clear, symmetrical breath sounds after orthopedic surgery point to a pulmonary embolism. The alveoli are ventilated but not perfused, which is a ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
Atelectasis usually develops gradually and causes diminished breath sounds or crackles in the bases, not clear lung fields with sudden symptoms.
A pneumothorax causes diminished or absent breath sounds and asymmetrical chest movement on the affected side. Neither is present.
Alveolar fluid, such as pulmonary edema, produces crackles. This client’s lungs are clear.
questions.rationale: Adequate oxygenation requires both inflated, well-oxygenated alveoli and well-perfused capillaries. When a blood clot blocks capillary blood flow, gas exchange fails even though the alveoli fill with air, so the client can be severely hypoxemic with clear breath sounds. Immobility after orthopedic surgery increases the risk of clots. A pulmonary angiogram or V/Q scan is used to look for the blocked blood flow.
questions.takeaway: Sudden hypoxemia with clear lungs means you should think perfusion, not ventilation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the two requirements for gas exchange from the module: inflated, well-oxygenated alveoli and well-perfused capillaries.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the normal findings as clues. Each wrong option predicts a lung-sound or chest-movement change that this client does not have.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Alterations: Hypoxemia and Hypoxia · Diagnostic Tests (ABGs)
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia is becoming irritable and reports feeling very tired. ABG results: pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 36 mm Hg, PaO₂ 58 mm Hg, SaO₂ 89%. Complete the statement by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The SaO₂ reports {0}, and the PaO₂ reports {1}. These results show {2}. If it is not corrected, it can progress to {3}.

options: the amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood
the percentage of hemoglobin bound to oxygen
the level of carbon dioxide in the blood
the acidity of the arterial blood
the percentage of hemoglobin bound to oxygen
the concentration of hemoglobin
the amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood
the rate and depth of breathing
hypercarbia
respiratory acidosis
hypocarbia
hypoxemia
hypoxia, decreased delivery of oxygen to the tissues
hypercarbia, retention of carbon dioxide
metabolic alkalosis
hyperventilation

questions.rationale: SaO₂ is the percentage of oxygen bound to hemoglobin, and PaO₂ is the amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood. The pH (7.35–7.45) and CO₂ (35–45 mm Hg) are normal, so there is no acid–base imbalance, hypercarbia, or hypocarbia. The low PaO₂ and SaO₂ show hypoxemia, a decreased level of oxygen in the blood. Left untreated, hypoxemia can lead to hypoxia, decreased delivery of oxygen to the tissues. Mild impairment causes fatigue, irritability, and discomfort, as this client shows.
questions.takeaway: SaO₂ = % of hemoglobin carrying O₂; PaO₂ = O₂ dissolved in blood. Hypoxemia (blood) leads to hypoxia (tissues).
questions.hintContent: Recall the module definitions of SaO₂ and PaO₂, and the difference between low oxygen in the blood and low oxygen in the tissues.
questions.hintStrategy: Check pH and CO₂ against their normal ranges first to rule out the acid–base options, then work through the oxygen values.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Airway Patency
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client in the postanesthesia care unit after general anesthesia is drowsy and difficult to arouse. The nurse hears loud snoring respirations and sees suprasternal retractions with little chest rise. SpO₂ has fallen from 96% to 89% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Increase the oxygen flow rate and recheck the SpO₂ in 10 minutes
Give the prescribed naloxone to reverse any residual opioid effect
Coach the client to take slow, deep breaths with the incentive spirometer
Open the airway with a head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust maneuver
optionRationales: Oxygen cannot reach the alveoli through an obstructed upper airway, and waiting 10 minutes allows hypoxemia to worsen.

Snoring with retractions signals mechanical obstruction by the relaxed tongue and soft tissues. Naloxone does not open the airway; it is considered only if hypoventilation persists once the airway is open.
A client who is difficult to arouse cannot perform incentive spirometry, and deep breathing does not relieve an upper-airway obstruction.

Correct. Snoring respirations and retractions in a sedated client indicate partial upper-airway obstruction from the tongue falling back. Repositioning the head and jaw is the immediate, independent action that restores airway patency.
questions.rationale: Airway patency comes first. After anesthesia or sedation, relaxed muscles let the tongue and soft tissues fall against the posterior pharynx, producing snoring respirations, retractions, and poor chest rise. The nurse opens the airway with a head-tilt/chin-lift (or jaw thrust if a cervical injury is possible), inserts an oral or nasal airway if needed, and then reassesses breathing and SpO₂ before considering other measures.
questions.takeaway: Snoring plus retractions in a sedated client means the airway is obstructed. Open it first.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens to the tongue and pharyngeal muscles in a sedated client, and which breath sound signals partial upper-airway obstruction.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do first. Apply the ABCs: choose the action that fixes the airway before actions that treat breathing or oxygenation.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · V/Q Mismatch
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the conditions of several clients with hypoxemia. For each condition, indicate whether it primarily impairs ventilation of the alveoli (airflow) or perfusion of the pulmonary capillaries (blood flow).
rows: A mucus plug obstructing the right lower lobe bronchus
A blood clot lodged in a branch of the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary edema from fluid volume excess
Destroyed alveolar walls and capillaries in emphysema
Postoperative atelectasis in the lung bases
optionRationales: Airflow problem. Sputum blocks air from reaching alveoli that are still perfused, so blood passes by without picking up oxygen.
Blood flow problem. The clot blocks capillary blood flow to alveoli that are still ventilated.
Airflow problem. Fluid in the alveoli prevents air from reaching the alveolar–capillary membrane.
Blood flow problem. The module lists emphysematous alveoli with the conditions that block capillary blood flow; the capillary bed around the damaged alveoli is lost.
Airflow problem. Collapsed alveoli receive no air even though blood continues to flow past them.
questions.rationale: The module divides V/Q alterations into two groups. In the first, airflow into the alveolus is blocked (sputum, inflammation, atelectasis, fluid volume excess). In the second, blood flow through the capillary is blocked (blood clots, plaque buildup, emphysematous alveoli). Either way, blood leaves the lungs without enough oxygen. Airflow problems respond to measures that open airways and alveoli, such as coughing, incentive spirometry, and positioning.
questions.takeaway: Airflow blocked (sputum, inflammation, collapse, fluid) vs blood flow blocked (clots, plaque, emphysema): both leave the blood unoxygenated.
questions.hintContent: For each condition, ask where the obstruction physically sits: in the airway or alveolus, or in the blood vessel.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each row independently. Visualize one alveolus and its capillary, and decide which side each condition blocks.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Postoperative Atelectasis

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Postoperative day 2, 1200: Client is 2 days postoperative after an open cholecystectomy with an upper abdominal incision. Rates incisional pain 7/10 and has been “too sore” to use the incentive spirometer. Reached 250 mL this morning (preoperative baseline 1,500 mL). Declined to ambulate this morning. Respirations shallow; client splints the abdomen. Breath sounds diminished in both bases. No cough or sputum. Chest expansion symmetrical. Calves soft and nontender. Last dose of prescribed oxycodone was 7 hours ago.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Pulmonary embolism
Atelectasis
Pneumothorax
Bacterial pneumonia
Give the prescribed analgesic, then coach incentive spirometry 10 times/hr while awake
Place the client flat supine to reduce tension on the incision
Assist the client to ambulate in the hall at least 3–4 times daily
Restrict oral fluids to reduce pulmonary congestion
Obtain a chest tube insertion tray for the bedside
Capillary blood glucose
Bowel sounds
SpO₂
Breath sounds in the lung bases
Urine specific gravity

condition: PE causes sudden hypoxemia, often with clear lung sounds. This client's gradual decline with shallow breathing and diminished bases fits collapsed alveoli better.

Correct. After upper abdominal surgery, pain causes shallow, splinted breathing and poor incentive spirometer use. The result is hypoventilation, alveolar collapse, diminished basilar breath sounds, and falling SpO₂. A normal WBC and absence of sputum argue against pneumonia.
A pneumothorax causes unilateral absent breath sounds and asymmetrical chest movement, often with sudden pleuritic pain. Findings here are bilateral and symmetrical.
Pneumonia usually causes productive cough, higher fever, and leukocytosis. The WBC is normal and the client has no cough or sputum.
actions: Correct. Controlling pain first allows deep breaths. Sustained maximal inspiration with the incentive spirometer (about 10 times per hour while awake) re-expands collapsed alveoli.
The flat supine position lowers lung volumes and worsens basilar collapse. Semi- to high-Fowler's position is better.
Correct. Early, frequent ambulation increases tidal volume and mobilizes secretions, which prevents and reverses atelectasis.
Fluid restriction thickens secretions and does not treat atelectasis, which is not caused by fluid overload.
Chest tubes treat air or fluid in the pleural space, not alveolar collapse.
parameters: Blood glucose does not reflect re-expansion of the alveoli.
Bowel sounds matter after abdominal surgery but do not show whether atelectasis is resolving.
Correct. Rising SpO₂ shows improved gas exchange as alveoli re-expand.
Correct. Return of breath sounds in the bases shows that previously collapsed alveoli are aerating.
Urine specific gravity reflects hydration status, not lung re-expansion.

questions.rationale: Postoperative atelectasis results from shallow breathing caused by incisional pain, immobility, and opioid effects, especially after upper abdominal and thoracic surgery. The cues are diminished basilar breath sounds, tachypnea, low-grade temperature elevation, and falling SpO₂ with poor incentive spirometer volumes. The nurse treats the cause by managing pain so the client can breathe deeply, coaching incentive spirometry, and ambulating the client. Progress is evaluated with SpO₂ and basilar breath sounds.
questions.takeaway: Postoperative atelectasis: treat pain, then inflate the lungs (incentive spirometry and walking), and watch SpO₂ and the bases.
questions.hintContent: Think about what upper abdominal incisional pain does to depth of breathing, and what happens to alveoli that are never fully inflated.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first, using the normal WBC and the bilateral, symmetrical findings to rule out options. Then choose actions and parameters that fit only that condition.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Physical Examination of the Chest
questions.stem: A client is admitted with right lower lobe pneumonia, and the chest x-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which findings should the nurse expect when assessing over the right lower lobe? Select all that apply.
options: Dullness on percussion
Bronchial breath sounds over the peripheral lung field
Increased tactile fremitus
Hyperresonance on percussion
Decreased tactile fremitus
Vesicular breath sounds with a long inspiratory phase
optionRationales: Correct. Consolidated, airless lung tissue is dense, so percussion is dull.
Correct. Solid tissue transmits sound from the large airways, so loud, high-pitched bronchial sounds are heard where soft vesicular sounds are normally expected.
Correct. Vibrations travel better through solid tissue than through air, so fremitus increases over consolidation.
Hyperresonance occurs over hyperinflated lung or air in the pleural space, as in emphysema or pneumothorax.
Fremitus decreases when air or fluid in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall, as in effusion or pneumothorax, not with consolidation.
Vesicular sounds with a longer inspiratory phase are the normal finding over peripheral lung fields.
questions.rationale: Consolidation replaces air in the alveoli with exudate, so the lung becomes dense. Dense tissue produces dull percussion, transmits voice vibrations better (increased fremitus), and carries bronchial breath sounds to areas where only vesicular sounds are normally heard. Findings of air, such as hyperresonance, or of a pleural barrier, such as decreased fremitus, point to other conditions.
questions.takeaway: Consolidation is solid: dull percussion, increased fremitus, and bronchial sounds in the wrong place.
questions.hintContent: Recall where each normal breath sound (bronchial, bronchovesicular, vesicular) is heard, and how sound travels through solid tissue versus air.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option as a separate true/false statement. Some options describe pairs of opposites, so only one of each pair can fit consolidation.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Adventitious Breath Sounds
questions.stem: The nurse auscultates the lungs of a client with chronic bronchitis and hears a loud, low-pitched, snoring sound over the trachea and bronchi on expiration that changes after the client coughs. Complete the statement by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The nurse should document this finding as {0}, which most likely indicates {1}.

options: stridor
rhonchi
fine crackles
pleural friction rub
fluid in the small airways and alveoli
upper airway narrowing at the larynx
secretions in the larger airways
inflamed pleural surfaces rubbing together

questions.rationale: Rhonchi (sometimes called sonorous wheezes) are low-pitched, snoring sounds produced by secretions in the trachea and bronchi. They often change or clear with coughing, which distinguishes them from other adventitious sounds. Stridor is a high-pitched inspiratory sound from upper airway narrowing. Fine crackles come from fluid or the opening of collapsed alveoli. A friction rub is a grating sound from inflamed pleura that does not clear with coughing.
questions.takeaway: Rhonchi are low-pitched snoring sounds from secretions in large airways, and they change with coughing.
questions.hintContent: Recall the adventitious sounds listed in the module (stridor, crackles, rhonchi, wheezing, pleural friction rub) and which one changes when secretions move.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the clues “low-pitched,” “large airways,” and “changes with coughing.” The second blank must describe the cause of the sound you chose in the first.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Signs of Hypoxia · Delegation
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN delegated vital signs to an assistive personnel (AP) on a medical unit. Which findings reported by the AP require the RN to assess the client immediately? Select all that apply.
options: An 82-year-old client whose respiratory rate is 18/min at rest
A client with pneumonia who is newly restless and trying to climb out of bed
A client with COPD whose SpO₂ is 90% on 2 L/min nasal cannula, the same as yesterday
A client who says, “I can’t catch my breath,” and can speak only 3–4 words at a time
A client whose SpO₂ dropped from 95% to 89% after walking and has not recovered after 5 minutes of rest
A client with a heart rate of 88/min who says the oxygen is drying out the lips
optionRationales: A respiratory rate of 15–20/min is expected for older adults.
Correct. New restlessness and confusion are early signs of hypoxia, especially in a client with pneumonia.
This SpO₂ is at the client's baseline and within a typical COPD target range.
Correct. Speaking in short phrases because of breathlessness indicates significant respiratory distress.
Correct. Desaturation that does not recover with rest suggests worsening gas exchange and needs RN assessment.
A normal heart rate and dry lips are comfort issues. The AP can offer a water-based lubricant.
questions.rationale: The AP collects data, but the RN must interpret it and act on unexpected findings. Early signs of hypoxia include restlessness, irritability, unexplained confusion, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Inability to speak in full sentences and desaturation that persists after rest also indicate an unstable client. Findings that are at baseline or expected for age can be addressed routinely.
questions.takeaway: The AP reports, the RN interprets. New restlessness, short phrases, and unresolved desaturation mean go now.
questions.hintContent: Recall the early signs of hypoxia listed in the module and normal respiratory rates across the lifespan.
questions.hintStrategy: For each report, ask whether it is new or unexpected, or baseline and expected. Only the new or unexpected findings need immediate RN assessment.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Signs of Hypoxia
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who is 2 days postoperative after abdominal surgery is restless, irritable, and pulling at the gown, and says, “I just feel really anxious.” HR 112/min, RR 26/min. The client asks for the prescribed PRN lorazepam. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer the lorazepam and reassess the client in 30 minutes
Check the SpO₂ and auscultate the client’s lung sounds
Encourage the client to call a family member for support
Dim the lights and reduce stimulation in the room
optionRationales: Sedating a client who may be hypoxic can depress respirations and hide worsening hypoxia.

Correct. Restlessness, irritability, anxiety, tachycardia, and tachypnea are early signs of hypoxia. The nurse must rule out a physiologic cause, such as atelectasis, PE, or pneumonia, before treating the behavior as anxiety.
Emotional support is appropriate only after a physiologic cause has been ruled out.
Reducing stimulation may help anxiety but delays assessment of a possible oxygenation problem.
questions.rationale: The module lists increasing restlessness, irritability, unexplained confusion, and rapid heart and respiratory rates as signs of hypoxia. Behavioral changes in a postoperative client must be treated as physiologic until proven otherwise. Assessment (SpO₂ and breath sounds) comes before intervention, and giving an anxiolytic first could be dangerous.
questions.takeaway: New “anxiety” with tachycardia and tachypnea is hypoxia until proven otherwise. Assess before you sedate.
questions.hintContent: Recall the early, subtle signs of hypoxia and why they are easy to mistake for psychological distress.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do first. Apply assessment before intervention, and physiologic needs before psychosocial ones.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Abnormal Breathing Patterns
questions.stem: A client admitted 6 hours ago with a traumatic brain injury had regular respirations of 16/min. The nurse now observes clusters of shallow breaths of varying depth with unpredictable apneic pauses of 15–20 seconds. The Glasgow Coma Scale score has dropped from 13 to 9. Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: The pattern suggests worsening brain injury that requires immediate provider notification
The client is sleeping deeply, which is expected during the first 24 hours after a head injury
The pattern is Kussmaul breathing caused by a developing metabolic acidosis
The client is hyperventilating in response to pain from the injury
optionRationales: Correct. Irregular, shallow breaths with periods of apnea (Biot, or ataxic, respirations) indicate CNS and brainstem dysfunction. With a falling GCS, this signals rising intracranial pressure and neurologic deterioration.
A GCS drop of 4 points is never an expected sleep finding. It is a major neurologic change.
Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid, and regular without apnea. It occurs in metabolic acidosis, not CNS injury.
Hyperventilation from pain is rapid and deep, without apnea, and would not explain the decline in consciousness.
questions.rationale: The module describes Biot respirations as shallow breathing with periods of apnea that occur in CNS disorders. A change from regular breathing to an irregular apneic pattern, together with a falling level of consciousness, indicates a worsening brain injury. This requires immediate provider notification and airway support.
questions.takeaway: A new irregular pattern with apnea plus a falling GCS means the brain is getting worse. Escalate now.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three abnormal patterns in the module (Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot) and the condition each is associated with.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the two changing cues, breathing pattern and GCS, and choose the hypothesis that explains both.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Sleep Apnea in Older Adults
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with obstructive sleep apnea is 1 day postoperative after a hip arthroplasty and is receiving oral oxycodone for pain. For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Assess respiratory rate, depth, and level of sedation before each opioid dose
Position the client flat supine for sleep
Use continuous pulse oximetry while the client is sleeping
Give the PRN zolpidem at bedtime in addition to the opioid
Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30°
optionRationales: Indicated. Opioids can cause hypoventilation; checking rate, depth, and sedation before each dose detects respiratory depression early.
Contraindicated. In the supine position the tongue and soft tissues fall back and worsen obstruction.
Indicated. Clients with OSA who receive opioids are at high risk for unrecognized respiratory depression, so continuous monitoring is recommended.
Contraindicated. Combining a sedative-hypnotic with an opioid adds to respiratory depression and upper-airway relaxation.
Indicated. Elevating the head of the bed or using lateral positioning reduces airway collapse and improves ventilation.
questions.rationale: Older adults have an increased risk of sleep apnea. Opioids depress the rate and depth of respirations and relax the upper-airway muscles, so this client is at high risk for hypoventilation, apnea, and hypoxemia during sleep. Safe care includes assessing breathing and sedation before each dose, continuous monitoring during sleep, head-up positioning, and avoiding additional sedating medications.
questions.takeaway: Sleep apnea + opioids: check breathing and sedation before each dose, keep the head up, monitor continuously, and add no extra sedatives.
questions.hintContent: Recall how opioids and sedatives affect respiratory drive and the muscles that keep the upper airway open.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each row on its own. Ask whether the intervention keeps the airway open and the client monitored, or adds to obstruction and sedation.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Breathing Techniques
questions.stem: The nurse taught pursed-lip breathing to a client with emphysema. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: “I breathe in slowly through my nose for about 2 counts.”
“I breathe out through puckered lips, taking about twice as long as I did breathing in.”
“I blow the air out as hard and fast as I can to empty my lungs.”
“I use this when I’m climbing stairs or start to feel short of breath.”
“I hold my breath for 30 seconds at the end of every breath.”
“This keeps my airways open longer so trapped air can get out.”
optionRationales: Correct. Slow inhalation through the nose warms, humidifies, and filters air.
Correct. Exhalation through pursed lips should take about twice as long as inhalation (for example, 2 counts in and 4 counts out).
Forceful exhalation increases intrathoracic pressure and causes small airways to collapse, which traps more air.
Correct. Pursed-lip breathing is used during exertion and dyspnea to control breathing and reduce air trapping.
Prolonged breath-holding is not part of the technique and can worsen dyspnea and CO₂ retention.
Correct. The gentle back-pressure keeps small airways open during exhalation so trapped air and CO₂ can escape.
questions.rationale: In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil lets small airways collapse during exhalation, which traps air. Pursed-lip breathing creates positive back-pressure that splints airways open, prolongs exhalation, slows the respiratory rate, and improves CO₂ elimination. Teaching is effective when the client describes slow nasal inhalation, gentle and prolonged pursed-lip exhalation, and use of the technique during exertion.
questions.takeaway: Smell the roses (in for 2), blow out the candle gently (out for 4). Never force it.
questions.hintContent: Recall why airways collapse during exhalation in emphysema and how gentle resistance at the lips counteracts that.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a positively worded SATA. Mark each statement true or false on its own, and be suspicious of statements that describe forceful or extreme breathing.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Abnormal Breathing Patterns
questions.stem: The nurse is documenting the breathing patterns of several clients. For each client, indicate which breathing pattern the nurse should document.
rows: A client with chronic kidney disease (pH 7.24, HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L) with deep, rapid, regular breaths at 30/min
A client with a large stroke and increased intracranial pressure whose breaths gradually deepen, then become shallower, followed by 20 seconds of apnea
A client with bacterial meningitis who has clusters of shallow breaths interrupted by irregular periods of apnea
A client with an opioid overdose whose breathing waxes and wanes in depth in a repeating cycle with periods of apnea
optionRationales: Kussmaul. Deep, rapid, regular respirations blow off CO₂ to compensate for metabolic acidosis, such as the acidosis of kidney failure.
Cheyne-Stokes. A crescendo–decrescendo pattern followed by apnea occurs with increased ICP, heart failure, and drug overdose.
Biot. Shallow breaths with irregular apneic periods occur in CNS disorders such as meningitis.
Cheyne-Stokes. The module lists drug overdose as a cause of the cyclic waxing and waning pattern with apnea.
questions.rationale: Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid, and regular without apnea, a compensation for metabolic acidosis. Cheyne-Stokes respiration cycles from deep, rapid breaths to slow, shallow breaths and then to apnea, and occurs with heart failure, increased ICP, and drug overdose. Biot respiration is shallow breathing with irregular apneic periods, and occurs with CNS disorders. Accurate documentation helps the team track neurologic and metabolic trends.
questions.takeaway: Kussmaul is deep and regular (acidosis). Cheyne-Stokes cycles with apnea. Biot is shallow and chaotic with apnea.
questions.hintContent: Recall how each pattern differs in depth, regularity, and the presence of apnea.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, look first for apnea (which rules out one pattern), then for a regular cycle versus chaotic clusters.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Hypoventilation After Chest Trauma
questions.stem: A client with three fractured ribs on the left is taking shallow breaths at 26/min and splinting the chest. The client rates pain 8/10. SpO₂ is 92% on room air, and breath sounds are diminished in the left base. Which plan will best improve the client’s breathing pattern?
options: Apply a tight elastic binder around the chest to stabilize the fractures
Keep the client on bed rest in the supine position until the pain improves
Limit deep breathing to prevent displacement of the fractured ribs
Give the prescribed analgesic, then coach deep breathing with splinting
optionRationales: Binding the chest restricts expansion and increases the risk of atelectasis and pneumonia. It is no longer recommended.
Immobility and the supine position reduce lung volumes and worsen basilar hypoventilation.
Avoiding deep breaths causes more atelectasis. Pain control, not restricted breathing, is the solution.
Correct. Pain is the cause of the shallow breathing. Adequate analgesia allows deep breaths, and incentive spirometry with pillow splinting re-expands the diminished base.
questions.rationale: Rib fractures cause pleuritic pain, so the client breathes shallowly (hypoventilation), which leads to atelectasis, retained secretions, and pneumonia. The priority is to treat the cause: effective pain control, followed by coached deep breathing, coughing with a splinting pillow, incentive spirometry, and early mobility. Chest binding and immobility worsen outcomes.
questions.takeaway: Rib fractures: treat the pain so the client can breathe. Never bind the chest.
questions.hintContent: Recall why a client in pain hypoventilates and what shallow breathing does to the alveoli in the bases.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the cause of the abnormal breathing pattern in the stem, then choose the plan that treats that cause and expands the lungs.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Arterial Blood Gas Sampling
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who is receiving anticoagulant therapy just had a radial arterial blood gas drawn. The respiratory therapist is called away to an emergency and asks the nurse to finish caring for the puncture site. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Apply firm direct pressure to the puncture site for at least 10 minutes
Apply a warm compress to the site to promote circulation to the hand
Elevate the arm above the heart and apply light pressure for 1 minute
Have the client open and close the fist repeatedly to restore blood flow
optionRationales: Correct. Arterial punctures need firm pressure for at least 5 minutes, and longer (commonly 10 minutes or more) for clients receiving anticoagulants, until bleeding stops. The site is then checked for hematoma and distal circulation.
Heat promotes vasodilation and bleeding at a fresh arterial puncture.
One minute of light pressure is not enough for an artery, especially in an anticoagulated client.
Hand movement increases arterial flow and can dislodge the forming clot.
questions.rationale: Arterial blood is under high pressure, so an ABG puncture site can bleed or form a hematoma. The risk is higher when the client takes an anticoagulant. Firm direct pressure is held for at least 5 minutes, and longer when the client is anticoagulated. The nurse then checks the site and assesses circulation, color, and sensation in the hand.
questions.takeaway: After an ABG, hold firm pressure for 5 minutes, and 10 minutes or more if the client is anticoagulated. Then check the hand.
questions.hintContent: Recall how arterial pressure differs from venous pressure and how anticoagulation affects clot formation.
questions.hintStrategy: Notice the key detail in the stem (anticoagulant therapy). Choose the option that best prevents bleeding at an arterial site.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Sputum Specimen
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with suspected pneumonia who needs a sputum specimen for culture and sensitivity. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Collect the specimen first thing in the morning when you wake up.”
“Rinse your mouth with plain water before you collect the specimen.”
“Use an antiseptic mouthwash first to get rid of bacteria in your mouth.”
“Take a few deep breaths, then cough deeply to bring up sputum from your lungs.”
“If you can’t cough anything up, spit saliva into the container instead.”
“We will collect the specimen before you receive your first dose of antibiotic.”
optionRationales: Correct. Secretions pool in the airways overnight, so an early-morning specimen gives the best yield.
Correct. Rinsing with water removes food particles and reduces contamination with oral bacteria.
Antiseptic mouthwash can kill organisms and interfere with culture results.
Correct. Deep breaths followed by a deep cough bring up sputum from the lower airways rather than saliva.
Saliva reflects oral flora, not lower-respiratory pathogens, and would be rejected or give misleading results.
Correct. Antibiotics given before collection can suppress organism growth and produce a false-negative culture.
questions.rationale: A sputum culture is useful only if the specimen comes from the lower respiratory tract and is not affected by antimicrobials. Best practice is an early-morning specimen, a water rinse (no mouthwash), and deep breathing and coughing into a sterile container, collected before antibiotics start and sent to the lab promptly. Saliva is not an acceptable substitute. The nurse may request an order for other methods, such as nebulized saline induction or suctioning, if the client cannot produce sputum.
questions.takeaway: Sputum culture: first thing in the morning, rinse with water only, cough from deep in the lungs, and collect before antibiotics.
questions.hintContent: Think about what could contaminate the specimen or kill the organism the lab is trying to grow.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each instruction separately. Ask whether it helps collect a true lower-airway sample or would contaminate or alter the specimen.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Thoracentesis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client had a thoracentesis 1 hour ago, and 900 mL of straw-colored fluid was removed from the right pleural space. Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Sudden sharp right-sided chest pain with increasing dyspnea
Absent breath sounds over the right upper lobe
Dry dressing at the puncture site with slight tenderness
SpO₂ decreased from 95% to 88% on room air
Breath sounds now heard in the right base, where they were diminished before
RR 18/min, and the client says breathing feels easier
optionRationales: Correct. Sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea after the procedure suggest a pneumothorax from lung puncture.
Correct. Absent breath sounds on the procedure side suggest air in the pleural space collapsing the lung.
A dry dressing with mild local tenderness is expected after the procedure.
Correct. A new drop in SpO₂ indicates impaired gas exchange and a possible complication.
Improved air entry in the base is the expected result of removing the effusion.
A normal respiratory rate and easier breathing show the procedure was effective.
questions.rationale: Thoracentesis removes pleural fluid to relieve compression of the lung. The most important complication is pneumothorax, which causes sudden pleuritic pain, dyspnea, diminished or absent breath sounds, asymmetrical chest movement, and desaturation. The nurse also watches the site for bleeding, and a chest x-ray is typically obtained afterward. Improved breath sounds and easier breathing indicate effective treatment.
questions.takeaway: After thoracentesis, watch for pneumothorax: sudden pain, dyspnea, lost breath sounds, and falling SpO₂.
questions.hintContent: Recall what structure the needle passes near during thoracentesis and what happens if air enters the pleural space.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding into expected improvement or new complication. Only the complications require immediate follow-up.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · ABG Interpretation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing ABG results for several clients. For each client, indicate the primary acid–base imbalance.
rows: A client who is oversedated after a procedure: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 55 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L
A client having a panic attack who is breathing 36/min: pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L
A client with diabetic ketoacidosis and Kussmaul respirations: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 25 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mEq/L
A client with COPD who became drowsy after a family member turned up the oxygen: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 64 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mEq/L
A client with kidney failure who has deep, rapid respirations: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 33 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L
optionRationales: Respiratory acidosis. Sedation depresses ventilation, CO₂ accumulates (PaCO₂ 55), and pH falls. HCO₃⁻ is normal, so there is no compensation yet.
Respiratory alkalosis. Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ (PaCO₂ 29), and pH rises.
Metabolic acidosis. Ketoacids consume bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ 10). The low PaCO₂ reflects Kussmaul compensation.
Respiratory acidosis. Excess oxygen in a client who retains CO₂ has worsened hypercarbia (PaCO₂ 64); the elevated HCO₃⁻ is the kidneys' chronic compensation.
Metabolic acidosis. Failing kidneys retain acid and lose bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ 16); the low PaCO₂ shows the lungs compensating.
questions.rationale: To identify the primary disorder, first classify the pH as acidotic or alkalotic. Then find which value explains it: a high PaCO₂ (above 45) matches acidosis and a low PaCO₂ (below 35) matches alkalosis (respiratory), while a low HCO₃⁻ matches acidosis (metabolic). Hypoventilation from sedation or CO₂ retention causes respiratory acidosis, hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, and acids from ketoacidosis or kidney failure cause metabolic acidosis, with the lungs compensating by lowering PaCO₂ (Kussmaul breathing).
questions.takeaway: Match the pH: PaCO₂ opposite the pH points to a respiratory cause, and HCO₃⁻ in the same direction as the pH points to a metabolic cause.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal ranges (pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45, HCO₃⁻ 22–26) and that CO₂ acts as an acid while HCO₃⁻ acts as a base.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the clinical context in each row as a second check. Ask whether the condition affects breathing (respiratory) or adds or removes acid (metabolic).

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Bronchoscopy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews the post-procedure note for a client who had a flexible bronchoscopy with biopsy. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.
questions.passage: A 61-year-old client returned from a flexible bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy under moderate sedation 1 hour ago. The client is {{drowsy but easily aroused}}, and the {{gag reflex has not yet returned}}. The client is expectorating {{a few streaks of blood in the sputum}} and reports {{a mild sore throat}}. From the doorway, the nurse hears {{a high-pitched crowing sound on inspiration}}. The client reports {{new sharp left-sided chest pain}}. Temperature {{37.6 °C (99.7 °F)}}, respiratory rate {{26/min}}, SpO₂ {{89% on 2 L/min nasal cannula}} (95% on room air before the procedure).
optionRationales: Expected. Residual sedation is normal 1 hour after moderate sedation when the client arouses easily.
Expected at this point. The topical anesthetic suppresses the gag reflex for 1–2 hours. The nurse keeps the client NPO until it returns, but this is not an abnormal finding.
Expected after biopsy. Small amounts of blood-streaked sputum are common. Frank bleeding would need follow-up.
Expected. Mild throat irritation from the scope is common and is treated with lozenges or gargles once the gag reflex returns.
Requires follow-up. Stridor indicates laryngeal edema or laryngospasm, an airway emergency.
Requires follow-up. New pleuritic chest pain after transbronchial biopsy suggests pneumothorax.
Expected. A low-grade temperature within 24 hours after bronchoscopy is common.
Requires follow-up. Tachypnea is new compared with baseline and supports respiratory compromise.
Requires follow-up. SpO₂ has fallen well below baseline despite supplemental oxygen.
questions.rationale: After bronchoscopy, the nurse monitors for airway compromise (laryngeal edema or laryngospasm, shown by stridor), pneumothorax (especially after transbronchial biopsy, shown by pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and desaturation), and significant bleeding. Mild sore throat, blood-streaked sputum, transient low-grade fever, residual sedation, and an absent gag reflex during the first 1–2 hours are expected. The client stays NPO until the gag reflex returns.
questions.takeaway: After bronchoscopy, stridor, new chest pain, tachypnea, and desaturation are red flags. A sore throat and blood streaks are expected.
questions.hintContent: Recall the expected effects of topical anesthesia, sedation, and biopsy after bronchoscopy, and the two most dangerous complications.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each finding is an expected consequence of the procedure or a sign of airway or lung compromise.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Oxygen Therapy in Chronic CO₂ Retention
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with COPD and chronic CO₂ retention is admitted with an exacerbation. The prescription reads “Titrate oxygen to maintain SpO₂ 88–92%.” A family member increased the flow to 6 L/min because the client “looked uncomfortable.” The client, who was alert an hour ago, is now difficult to arouse. SpO₂ 98%, RR 12/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to cough and take several slow, deep breaths
Raise the head of the bed and apply a nonrebreather mask
Reduce the oxygen to the prescribed target and notify the provider
Allow the client to rest, because the SpO₂ shows adequate oxygenation
optionRationales: A client who is difficult to arouse cannot effectively cough and deep breathe on command, and this does not remove the cause.
A nonrebreather would deliver even more oxygen and worsen hypercapnia.

Correct. Excess oxygen in a client who retains CO₂ can worsen V/Q mismatch and reduce ventilation, causing hypercapnia and CO₂ narcosis. The nurse titrates down to the 88–92% target (without abruptly stopping oxygen), notifies the provider, and anticipates an ABG.
A high SpO₂ with new somnolence suggests rising CO₂. Letting the client sleep ignores a dangerous change in LOC.
questions.rationale: Clients who chronically retain CO₂ can develop hypercapnic respiratory acidosis when given uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen. This is why a target range of 88–92% is prescribed. New drowsiness after an oxygen increase indicates CO₂ narcosis. The nurse reduces oxygen to the target without discontinuing it, since abrupt removal can cause rebound hypoxemia, then notifies the provider and anticipates an ABG. Oxygen should never be withheld from a hypoxemic client with COPD. It should be titrated.
questions.takeaway: COPD with CO₂ retention: aim for 88–92%. More oxygen is not better, and new drowsiness means check the CO₂.
questions.hintContent: Recall the usual SpO₂ target for clients with chronic CO₂ retention and what happens when they receive uncontrolled high-flow oxygen.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the current SpO₂ with the prescribed range and connect it to the change in level of consciousness. Then choose the action that corrects the cause.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Oxygen Safety and Device Checks
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse makes hourly rounds on a client receiving continuous oxygen by nasal cannula at 4 L/min as prescribed. Click to highlight the findings that require the nurse to take action.
questions.passage: The {{flowmeter ball is centered on the 4 L/min line}}. The {{oxygen tubing is pinched under the bed's side rail}}. The client's {{SpO₂ is 91%, down from 95% an hour ago}}. The {{skin behind both ears is reddened and tender}} where the tubing rests. The {{humidifier bottle is filled to the line}}, and {{the curved prongs point downward into the nares}}. A visitor is {{applying a petroleum-based balm to the client's lips}}. The client is {{breathing through the mouth while watching television}}.
optionRationales: No action needed. The flow matches the prescription, and the reading is taken from the center of the ball.
Action needed. Kinked or pinched tubing blocks oxygen delivery and should be freed right away.
Action needed. A falling SpO₂ needs assessment and correction of the cause, which here is likely the occluded tubing.
Action needed. Device-related pressure injury is developing. Pad the tubing over the ears and assess the skin regularly.
No action needed. The humidifier is correctly filled; humidification is appropriate at flows of about 4 L/min or more.
No action needed. Curved prongs should point downward, following the natural curve of the nasal passages.
Action needed. Petroleum-based products are flammable in an oxygen-enriched environment and can irritate the airways. Use a water-based lubricant.
No action needed. Oxygen pools in the nasopharynx, so a client who breathes through the mouth still receives oxygen from a nasal cannula.
questions.rationale: Oxygen safety checks include flow rate, patent tubing, device fit, skin integrity at pressure points, humidification, fire safety, and the client's response. Kinked tubing, falling SpO₂, early device-related pressure injury behind the ears, and petroleum products near oxygen all need prompt action. Correct flow, correct prong orientation, a filled humidifier, and mouth breathing with a cannula are acceptable.
questions.takeaway: Oxygen rounds: check the flow, check the tubing, check the skin behind the ears, and keep petroleum away.
questions.hintContent: Recall the elements of an oxygen safety check: flow, patency, fit, skin, humidity, fire safety, and the client's response.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each highlighted phrase on its own. Ask whether it is correct as-is or a problem you must fix.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Evaluating Oxygen Therapy
questions.stem: One hour ago, the oxygen for a client with pneumonia was increased to 6 L/min by nasal cannula. Which findings indicate that the current oxygen therapy is not effective and should be reported to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: SpO₂ 87%
RR 32/min with use of accessory muscles
New restlessness and confusion
Client speaks in full sentences
Heart rate decreased from 118/min to 96/min
Warm, dry skin with pink oral mucosa
optionRationales: Correct. SpO₂ remains well below target despite the maximum practical nasal cannula flow, so the client likely needs a higher-concentration device or other support.
Correct. Tachypnea with accessory muscle use indicates continued high work of breathing.
Correct. New changes in mental status are signs of worsening cerebral hypoxia.
Speaking in full sentences suggests adequate air movement.
A falling heart rate toward normal suggests improved oxygen delivery.
Pink oral mucosa and warm skin indicate adequate central oxygenation and perfusion.
questions.rationale: Evaluating oxygen therapy means looking for changes in SpO₂, respiratory rate and effort, heart rate, mental status, and skin and mucosa color. A nasal cannula tops out at about 6 L/min (about 44% FiO₂). If the client remains hypoxemic, tachypneic, and newly confused at that flow, the therapy is ineffective and needs escalation, such as a higher-FiO₂ device, high-flow nasal cannula, or ventilatory support.
questions.takeaway: If SpO₂, work of breathing, and mental status do not improve on 6 L/min by nasal cannula, escalate.
questions.hintContent: Recall the maximum useful flow of a nasal cannula and the assessment findings that show whether hypoxia is improving.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding as improved or not improved. Select only the ones showing that the client is still hypoxic.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Foreign Object in the Airway
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant eating a snack suddenly cannot cry or cough and has bluish lips but is still conscious. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Confirm that the infant cannot cry or cough and call for help
Hold the infant face down along the forearm with the head lower than the chest, supporting the head and jaw
Deliver up to 5 forceful back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand
Turn the infant face up, supporting the head, keeping the head lower than the trunk
Deliver up to 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the sternum, just below the nipple line
questions.rationale: Infants are at high risk for foreign-body airway obstruction because their airways are short and narrow. For a conscious infant with a severe obstruction (unable to cry or cough), the rescuer delivers 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts and repeats the cycle until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive. Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of liver injury. If the infant becomes unresponsive, the rescuer begins CPR and looks in the mouth for the object before giving breaths.
questions.takeaway: Choking infant: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, head down. No abdominal thrusts.
questions.hintContent: Recall how infant foreign-body obstruction relief differs from the technique used for older children and adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Start by confirming a severe obstruction, then think about positioning before each set of maneuvers.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Foreign Object in the Airway
questions.stem: A 2-year-old is brought to urgent care after a sudden episode of coughing and gagging while eating trail mix with peanuts 3 hours ago. The child has no fever and no recent respiratory illness. The nurse hears an intermittent cough and wheezing only over the right side, with diminished breath sounds in the right lower lobe. SpO₂ is 95%. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Foreign-body aspiration into the right bronchus
A viral upper respiratory infection
New-onset asthma triggered by a food allergen
Bacterial pneumonia of the right lower lobe
optionRationales: Correct. A sudden choking episode while eating small, hard food, followed by unilateral wheezing and diminished breath sounds, is classic for aspiration. The right bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical, so objects usually lodge there.
Upper respiratory infections are common in children but develop over days with a runny nose and often fever; they do not begin with sudden choking or cause one-sided wheezing.
Asthma causes bilateral, diffuse wheezing, typically with triggers and recurrent episodes.
Pneumonia develops over days with fever and is not preceded by a sudden choking event.
questions.rationale: Toddlers are at high risk for aspirating foreign objects, and nuts, popcorn, and grapes are common culprits. Children may appear stable after the initial choking episode, then develop localized findings: unilateral wheeze, diminished breath sounds, and cough. Because of airway anatomy, the object usually enters the right mainstem bronchus. Suspected aspiration requires imaging and removal by bronchoscopy.
questions.takeaway: A sudden choking episode plus one-sided wheezing is a foreign body, usually on the right, until proven otherwise.
questions.hintContent: Recall why children are at higher risk for airway obstruction and which bronchus foreign objects most often enter.
questions.hintStrategy: Focus on the timing (sudden onset while eating) and the location (one side only). Rule out diagnoses that are bilateral or develop over days.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Pregnancy
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the triage note for a pregnant client. Click to highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.passage: A client at 30 weeks' gestation reports 2 days of fever, cough, and body aches; a rapid influenza test is positive. She reports {{nasal stuffiness that began early in pregnancy}} and {{mild shortness of breath when climbing stairs over the past month}}. She had {{a small nosebleed yesterday}} and notices {{occasional painless tightening of the abdomen}}. Temperature {{38.9 °C (102 °F)}}, respiratory rate {{28/min}}, SpO₂ {{93% on room air}}, fetal heart rate {{172/min}}.
optionRationales: Expected. Rhinitis of pregnancy is caused by estrogen-related mucosal edema.
Expected. The rising uterus elevates the diaphragm, and increased respiratory drive commonly causes mild exertional dyspnea.
Expected. Increased vascularity of the nasal mucosa makes nosebleeds common in pregnancy.
Expected. Painless, irregular Braxton Hicks contractions are normal in the third trimester.
Requires follow-up. High maternal fever increases fetal oxygen demand and heart rate and should be treated promptly (for example, with acetaminophen).
Requires follow-up. Respiratory rate rises only slightly in pregnancy. A rate of 28/min indicates respiratory distress.
Requires follow-up. Pregnant clients should maintain SpO₂ of at least 95% to protect fetal oxygenation. Pregnancy lowers oxygen reserve, so desaturation can progress quickly.
Requires follow-up. A fetal heart rate above 160/min is fetal tachycardia, which may reflect maternal fever or hypoxemia.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy raises the diaphragm, reduces functional residual capacity, and increases oxygen consumption, so pregnant clients desaturate more quickly and are at high risk for severe influenza. The nurse must distinguish normal adaptations (nasal congestion, epistaxis, mild dyspnea of pregnancy, Braxton Hicks contractions) from warning signs: fever, tachypnea, SpO₂ below 95%, and fetal tachycardia. Prompt treatment involving both obstetric and pulmonary providers protects mother and fetus.
questions.takeaway: In pregnancy, keep SpO₂ at 95% or higher. Fever, tachypnea, and fetal tachycardia need action. A stuffy nose and mild dyspnea on stairs are normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal respiratory changes of pregnancy from the lifespan content and the minimum maternal SpO₂ needed to protect the fetus.
questions.hintStrategy: For each phrase, decide whether it is a normal pregnancy adaptation or a sign that the mother or fetus is compromised.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Older Adults
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with gastroesophageal reflux disease and a weakened cough reflex is being discharged after treatment for aspiration pneumonia. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I’ll use my incentive spirometer and cough deeply several times a day.”
“I’ll raise the head of my bed on blocks when I sleep at night.”
“I’ll take small bites and avoid talking while I’m chewing.”
“I’ll lie down for a short nap right after lunch to help my digestion.”
optionRationales: This statement is correct. Incentive spirometry and effective coughing help clear secretions and are recommended for older adults.
This statement is correct. Elevating the head of the bed reduces nighttime reflux and aspiration.
This statement is correct. Small bites and not talking while eating reduce choking risk when the cough reflex is diminished.
Correct (needs further teaching). Lying down after eating promotes reflux and aspiration. The client should stay upright for 2–3 hours after meals.
questions.rationale: Aging reduces the cough and gag reflexes, and GERD becomes more common, both of which increase the risk of aspiration and pneumonia in older adults. Teaching focuses on upright positioning during and after meals, elevating the head of the bed, careful eating habits, effective coughing, and incentive spirometry. Lying down soon after a meal undermines these precautions.
questions.takeaway: Older adults with GERD and a weak cough should stay upright after meals. Lying down right after eating invites aspiration.
questions.hintContent: Recall the age-related changes in cough reflex and the GERD-related risks listed for older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item. Find the statement that is incorrect or unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Pediatric Respiratory Distress
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 2-year-old with a respiratory infection. Which findings indicate respiratory distress requiring immediate intervention? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory rate of 32/min while awake and playing
Head bobbing with each breath
Mostly abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing at rest
Suprasternal and intercostal retractions
Inspiratory stridor while calm
Expiratory grunting
optionRationales: A rate of 20–40/min is normal for a toddler, especially during activity.
Correct. Head bobbing shows accessory neck muscle use in a young child and indicates significant distress.
Children younger than 6 breathe mainly with the diaphragm, so abdominal breathing is expected.
Correct. Retractions show that the child is generating high negative pressure to move air, a sign of increased work of breathing.
Correct. Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway narrowing.
Correct. Grunting is an attempt to keep alveoli open by exhaling against a partly closed glottis, a sign of severe distress.
questions.rationale: Children have narrower airways and less respiratory reserve, so they can deteriorate quickly. Warning signs of respiratory distress include retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting, stridor at rest, and cyanosis. Normal findings for age, such as diaphragmatic breathing before age 6 and a toddler's rate of 20–40/min, must be recognized so they are not mistaken for distress.
questions.takeaway: In young children, head bobbing, retractions, grunting, and stridor at rest mean distress. Belly breathing is normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal respiratory rate for toddlers and the age at which children stop breathing mainly with the diaphragm.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide for each finding whether it is expected for a 2-year-old or a sign of increased work of breathing.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Newborns
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a term newborn 2 hours after birth. Which finding requires follow-up?
options: Respiratory rate of 52/min, irregular, with pauses of 5–10 seconds
Bluish discoloration of the hands and feet with a pink trunk
Audible expiratory grunting with nasal flaring
Abdomen rising with each breath while the chest moves little
optionRationales: A rate of 30–60/min with irregular periodic breathing and pauses under 20 seconds is normal in newborns.
Acrocyanosis with a pink trunk is common in the first 24–48 hours and does not indicate central hypoxemia.
Correct. Grunting and nasal flaring are signs of respiratory distress, which may reflect transient tachypnea, respiratory distress syndrome, or infection.
Newborns breathe mainly with the diaphragm, so abdominal movement is expected.
questions.rationale: Newborns normally breathe 30–60 times per minute with an irregular, periodic pattern and brief pauses of less than 20 seconds. Their breathing is diaphragmatic, and acrocyanosis is common. Grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, central cyanosis, and apnea of 20 seconds or longer are abnormal and require prompt evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Newborns: irregular breathing at 30–60/min and blue hands are normal. Grunting and flaring are not.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal newborn respiratory rate and pattern, and which color changes are expected shortly after birth.
questions.hintStrategy: Three options describe normal newborn adaptations. Find the one that signals increased work of breathing.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Independent Interventions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with COPD becomes dyspneic during morning care. SpO₂ is 90% on 2 L/min nasal cannula, and the prescribed target range is 88–92%. Which independent nursing interventions should the nurse include to improve the client’s breathing pattern? Select all that apply.
options: Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler's position
Schedule rest periods between bathing, grooming, and dressing
Coach pursed-lip breathing during exertion
Give an extra dose of albuterol from the client's inhaler
Increase the oxygen to 5 L/min during activity
Direct a handheld fan toward the client's face
optionRationales: Correct. Upright positioning lowers the diaphragm and improves lung expansion. The nurse can do this independently.
Correct. Spacing activities lowers oxygen demand and prevents exhaustion (monitoring activity tolerance and assisting with ADLs).
Correct. Pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation, reduces air trapping, and slows the respiratory rate.
Extra medication doses need a prescription. This is a collaborative intervention.
Changing oxygen flow needs a prescription or protocol, and 5 L/min could push SpO₂ above the target range.
Correct. Airflow across the face stimulates trigeminal receptors and reduces the sensation of breathlessness. This is an evidence-based, nonpharmacologic measure.
questions.rationale: Independent nursing interventions to improve gas exchange and breathing patterns include positioning, breathing techniques, pacing activities, assisting with ADLs, promoting secretion clearance, and comfort measures such as a handheld fan. Medications and changes to oxygen therapy are collaborative and need a prescription or protocol. SpO₂ is already within the prescribed range.
questions.takeaway: Independent dyspnea measures: sit the client up, pace activities, use pursed-lip breathing, and use a fan. Medications and oxygen changes need orders.
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between independent and collaborative interventions, and the examples of independent interventions listed in the module.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option for two things: does it help the breathing pattern, and can the nurse do it without a prescription?

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Lifespan: Older Adults · NGN Case Study: Older Adult with Pneumonia
questions.stem: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for an 82-year-old client. Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Click to highlight the assessment findings that require follow-up.
questions.passage: The client is {{oriented to person only (baseline: oriented ×3)}}. The nurse notes {{mild kyphosis}}, {{fine inspiratory crackles at both bases that clear after coughing}}, and {{crackles that do not clear with coughing and diminished breath sounds over the right lower lobe}}. Temperature {{37.2 °C (99.0 °F)}}, heart rate {{112/min}}, respiratory rate {{28/min}}, SpO₂ {{89% on room air}}. The oral mucosa is {{dry}}.
questions.rationale: Older adults often present with pneumonia atypically — with new confusion, weakness, loss of appetite, tachycardia, and tachypnea, and often without a fever. The nurse must also know which findings are expected with aging: kyphosis, slightly decreased breath sounds, and inspiratory crackles at the bases are common. Findings that are new or localized (confusion below baseline, crackles and diminished sounds over one lobe, tachycardia, tachypnea, low SpO₂, and signs of poor fluid intake) require follow-up.
optionRationales: Requires follow-up. New confusion compared with baseline is a common atypical sign of pneumonia and of hypoxia in older adults.
Expected. Kyphosis is a common age-related change that the nurse assesses for; it is not new.
Expected. Inspiratory crackles at the bases are common in older adults, and these clear with coughing.
Requires follow-up. Localized crackles that do not clear and diminished breath sounds over one lobe suggest consolidation from pneumonia.
Does not require follow-up. The temperature is normal; older adults with pneumonia often have no fever.
Requires follow-up. Tachycardia is an early sign of hypoxia and a common atypical sign of pneumonia.
Requires follow-up. A rate of 28/min is above the expected 15–20/min for older adults.

questions.rationale: New confusion, weakness, poor appetite, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, localized right lower lobe crackles, an elevated WBC, and a right lower lobe infiltrate point to pneumonia, even without fever. questions.stem: The client is being admitted to the medical unit. Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Orders. Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Obtain the sputum and blood cultures, then give the first antibiotic dose without delay
Titrate oxygen to keep the SpO₂ at 92% or higher
Keep the head of the bed at 30° or higher
Suction the oropharynx as needed when secretions pool
Offer thin liquids through a straw to correct dehydration before the swallow screen
Apply wrist restraints to manage the confusion
Hold the IV fluids until the client is drinking well
questions.rationale: Care combines collaborative and independent interventions. Cultures are obtained before the first antibiotic dose so the organism can be identified, and the antibiotic follows promptly. Oxygen is titrated to the prescribed target. Because older adults have decreased gag and cough reflexes, the nurse elevates the head of the bed and suctions as needed to protect the airway. Nothing is given by mouth until the swallow screen is done, IV fluids correct the fluid deficit, and confusion from hypoxia is treated by correcting the cause, not by restraints.
optionRationales: Correct. Cultures come first so antibiotics do not interfere with identifying the organism; the antibiotic is then given promptly.
Correct. Oxygen administration is indicated by the low SpO₂ and is titrated to the prescribed target.
Correct. Upright positioning improves lung expansion and reduces the risk of aspirating reflux.
Correct. The module lists frequent suctioning for older adults because of a decreased gag and cough reflex.
Oral fluids before a swallow screen risk further aspiration, and straws increase the risk in a client who recently choked.
Confusion here is likely caused by hypoxia and infection; restraints increase agitation and do not treat the cause.
IV fluids are prescribed because intake is poor and the BUN is elevated; holding them worsens the fluid deficit and thickens secretions.
questions.takeaway: Older adult with pneumonia: cultures then antibiotics, titrated O₂, HOB up, suction as needed, nothing by mouth until the swallow screen.
questions.hintContent: Consider the older adult's decreased gag and cough reflex and the collaborative orders that treat the infection and the hypoxemia.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own: does it treat the infection, improve oxygenation, or protect the airway — or does it add a new risk?

questions.stem: The nurse reassesses the client after admission. Refer to the 1100 entry in the Nurses' Notes. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min and recheck the SpO₂ in 15 minutes
Suction the mouth and pharynx with a Yankauer catheter, then reassess
Offer small sips of water to help the client clear the throat
Notify the provider to request a repeat chest x-ray
questions.rationale: Airway comes first. Older adults have a decreased gag and cough reflex, so secretions pool and are easily aspirated; the module lists frequent suctioning for this reason. With secretions visible in the mouth and gurgling respirations, the nurse clears the airway with oropharyngeal (Yankauer) suctioning, keeps the head of the bed elevated or turns the client to the side, and then reassesses breath sounds and SpO₂.
optionRationales: More oxygen does not remove the secretions blocking the airway, and waiting 15 minutes increases the risk of aspiration.
Correct. Oropharyngeal suctioning is the least invasive way to clear secretions that are visible in the mouth and pharynx. The nurse then reassesses.
Oral fluids for a client with a weak cough and pooled secretions greatly increase the risk of aspiration; the swallow screen has not been done.
A chest x-ray may be needed later, but the first action is to clear the airway.
questions.takeaway: Gurgling and pooled secretions in an older adult with a weak cough: suction first, then reassess.
questions.hintContent: Recall why older adults with a decreased gag and cough reflex need frequent suctioning.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify where the problem is (the upper airway) and choose the action that clears it before actions that add oxygen or gather data.
